headline: Tea may help your heart, but let it cool first

sources.title: How you drink your tea could determine whether you gain or lose heart health benefits (CNN, via CP24)
Tea Drinkers May Have Fewer Heart and Blood Vessel Problems, Large Study Finds (Sci.News)
Regular tea consumption linked to lower risk of vascular disease (News-Medical)

chunks.text: A cup of tea may help your heart, but how hot you drink it seems to matter. That is the finding of a large study that {{came out}} on October 21, 2026, in the Journal of Internal Medicine. Researchers from Peking Union Medical College in China followed about 485,000 adults for about nine years. Everyone described their [[tea-drinking habits]] [[in detail]].

verbs.correct: To be published for people to read
verbs.wrong: To be checked by other scientists
verbs.why: A new phone comes out every fall. Her first book comes out in May. That is the finding of a large study that came out on October 21, 2026, in the Journal of Internal Medicine.

chunks.text: People who drank tea at least three days a week had about an 11 percent lower [[risk]] of heart and [[blood vessel]] disease. Tea drinkers who did not smoke and {{worked out}} a lot did best of all. But one result {{stood out}}. People who drank their tea "burning hot" had a 16 percent higher risk than people who did not drink tea regularly. Tea at [[room temperature]] or hot, but not [[scalding]], was linked to lower risk.

verbs.wrong: To eat a lot of fresh food
verbs.why: My dad works out at the gym three times a week. She works out every morning before her job. Tea drinkers who did not smoke and worked out a lot did best of all.
A bright yellow house stands out on a gray street. Her red coat always stands out in a crowd. But one result stood out.

chunks.text: The study shows a [[link]], not proof that tea protects the heart. People reported their own habits, so one person's "burning hot" may be another person's "warm." The study cannot {{rule out}} other differences, such as diet or [[income]]. Outside experts {{weighed in}}. A [[dietitian]] at a British [[heart charity]] said differences in diet and [[lifestyle]] could help explain the results. An American emergency doctor, a health expert for a TV news network, says tea contains natural [[compounds]] that may help {{bring down}} [[blood pressure]].

verbs.correct: To show that something is not a cause
verbs.wrong: To check something more than once
verbs.why: Doctors take an X-ray to rule out a broken bone. Mechanics test the battery to rule out a simple problem. The study cannot rule out other differences, such as diet or income.

verbs.correct: To share an opinion about something
verbs.wrong: To repeat what others have said
verbs.why: Parents often weigh in on the school lunch menu. Everyone weighs in when our family plans a trip. Outside experts weighed in.

Big sales bring down the price of winter coats. Lower taxes bring down the cost of food. An American emergency doctor, a health expert for a TV news network, says tea contains natural compounds that may help bring down blood pressure.

chunks.text: The American doctor has simple advice. Tea lovers do not need to {{cut out}} their favorite drink. They should avoid tea hot enough to burn the mouth or throat. Instead, they can {{hold off}} until it {{cools down}} enough to sip [[comfortably]]. Choosing [[unsweetened]] tea can help people {{cut back on}} [[sugary drinks]]. People who do not drink tea do not need to start. Exercise, a healthy diet and not smoking also protect the heart.

verbs.correct: To stop eating or drinking something
verbs.why: Some athletes cut out fried food before a big race. Many people cut out sugar when they want to lose weight. Tea lovers do not need to cut out their favorite drink.

verbs.wrong: To add cold milk to a drink
verbs.why: We hold off on dinner until everyone arrives. Farmers hold off on planting when the ground is too cold. Instead, they can hold off until it cools down enough to sip comfortably.
Hot soup cools down in a few minutes. A car engine cools down after a long drive. Instead, they can hold off until it cools down enough to sip comfortably.

verbs.wrong: To mix one thing with another
verbs.why: Doctors tell many patients to cut back on salt. She cuts back on coffee during exam week. Choosing unsweetened tea can help people cut back on sugary drinks.

mainIdea.s: A huge study in China linked regular tea drinking to a lower risk of heart disease. People who drank their tea burning hot had a higher risk, so a doctor says to let it cool first.
mainIdea.why: Regular tea drinkers had about an 11 percent lower risk, but one result stood out. Burning hot tea came with a higher risk, so people should hold off before sipping.

mainIdea.s: Scientists in China have proven that regular tea drinking keeps the heart safe from disease. They now advise people who never touch tea to start, as long as each cup is not too hot.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the study shows only a link, not proof. The doctor also says people who do not drink tea do not need to start.

mainIdea.s: A new study from Japan found that green tea helps older adults sleep better at night. Researchers say a warm cup before bed may calm the mind and make it easier to fall asleep.
mainIdea.why: This story is about tea and heart disease in China. A study that came out in October linked tea to a lower risk, unless the tea is burning hot.

tf.s: A large study about tea and heart health came out in a medical journal.
tf.why: The study came out in the Journal of Internal Medicine. Researchers in China followed about 485,000 adults for about nine years.

tf.s: People who drank their tea burning hot had the lowest risk of heart disease.
tf.why: That result stood out for the opposite reason. People who drank burning hot tea had a higher risk than people who did not drink tea regularly.

tf.s: Regular tea drinkers had a lower risk of heart and blood vessel disease.
tf.why: They had about an 11 percent lower risk. Tea drinkers who did not smoke and worked out a lot had the lowest risk of all.

tf.s: The study proves that drinking tea protects the heart.
tf.why: It shows a link, not proof. The study cannot rule out other differences, such as diet or income.

tf.s: An American doctor says people should hold off until their tea is cool enough to sip.
tf.why: She says people should avoid tea hot enough to burn the mouth or throat and wait until they can sip it comfortably.

tf.s: The American doctor says tea lovers need to cut out their favorite drink.
tf.why: She says they do not need to cut it out. They can simply let it cool down before they sip it.

lines.text: Do you drink your tea [[piping hot]]?
A big study about tea and the heart {{came out}} in October.
Mostly good. Regular tea drinkers had a lower risk of heart disease.
That sounds [[too good to be true]].
Well, it shows a link, not proof. The researchers can't {{rule out}} other reasons, like diet.
I see. So what's the bad news?
One result {{stood out}}. People who drank their tea burning hot had a higher risk.
Oh no. Do I have to {{cut out}} my morning tea?
No. Just {{hold off}} for a few minutes and let it {{cool down}}.
Exactly. A good [[rule of thumb]] is to wait until you can sip it comfortably.
What about sugar? I put two spoons in every cup.
Unsweetened tea is better. It can help you {{cut back on}} sugar.
Should people who don't drink tea start drinking it?
Not at all. They can {{work out}} and eat well instead. That's good news for me, because tea isn't really [[my cup of tea]].

expressions.def: A simple guide that works most of the time
ex: A good rule of thumb is to drink water with every meal.

expressions.def: Something you like or enjoy, often used with not
ex: Horror movies are not my cup of tea.
